newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Challenger cries foul in Moldova presidential vote.
newsitem.headline: Challenger cries foul in Moldova presidential vote.

text.p: Moldovans voted in the second round of the former Soviet republic's first multi-candidate presidential election on Sunday and the left-wing challenger accused President Mircea Snegur of plotting to rig the ballot.
"People have been paid to vote. Other inventions to falsify the results are being used," parliament chairman Petru Lucinschi said after voting in the capital Chisinau.

Lucinschi, who won 28 percent in the November 17 first round and who is neck-and-neck with Snegur in opinion polls for the run-off, also told reporters he feared Snegur's supporters could take to the streets, aided by the police.
But reporters saw no gatherings by early afternoon.
Raisa Pashenko, an observer for Lucinschi at Chisinau's polling station No 119, expected a fair count in the capital. But she added: "Out in the country they might fix it."

Turnout was 10.5 percent by 11 a.m. (0900 GMT), slightly down on the first round. Analysts say a low turnout favours Snegur, who is strong in heavy-voting rural areas where a majority of the 4.3 million Moldovans live.
Observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) had also reported no significant violations.

OSCE coordinator Kare Vollan said observers were paying attention to polling stations close to the Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 fearing Moldovans wanted to unite with ethnic kin in Romania.
Authorities in the 700,000-strong area, where hundreds died in fighting in 1992, are ignoring the poll but they say local people can vote elsewhere.

Snegur, president since independence in 1991, accused Lucinschi, whose backers include state television, much of the press and the Moldovan Orthodox Church, of "illegal methods including mudslinging in the press, libel and rumours".
Pledging to press on with market reforms, the 56-year-old Snegur polled 39 percent in the first round and has been endorsed by pro-Romanian nationalists.
But he faces stiff opposition. Both Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, knocked out in the first round, and the communists, support Lucinschi.
Sangheli, who blocked an attempt by Snegur to sack the defence minister last March, says he will resign after the election "to preserve civil peace".
The president's bluff man-of-the-people image wins favour in the countryside. But the deep economic crisis of the past five years has fuelled support for the intellectual Lucinschi.
"I'm for Lucinschi," said Valya as she swept autumn leaves in front of her single-storey Chisinau house. "My pension's only 50 lei (about $10) a month and I don't always get it."
But there is no shortage of Snegur loyalists.
"I'm for Snegur. He gave us our independence, he knows what to do," said Glavya, a Chisinau housewife in her 40s. "The problem is the government don't let him do what needs to."

Snegur wants greater powers to carry out reforms. He dismisses fears among the one-third Russian minority that he might unite with Romania, from whose territory Stalin carved most of Moldova in World War Two.
Lucinschi, also 56 and like the president a top communist in Soviet times, presents himself as a social democrat.
He accuses Snegur of stirring up bloody fighting in Dnestr. Playing down links with Bucharest, he reminds Moldovans they depend on Russia for their energy.
Some 2.4 million electors have until 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) to vote. A preliminary result is expected after midnight.
